Not really the same. Film is closer to gaming than music, but there are still too many differences to copy another industry’s model. For example, music pays artists per stream, but film does not. That difference comes down to how contracts have traditionally worked. Music contracts were based on sales numbers, with labels taking on little risk, so per-stream payments made sense. Film usually works with lump-sum contracts where the studio fronts the costs and hopes to earn it back later. Games are closer to film, but you don't have platforms vying to buy your product towards the end of production. Typically games have target platforms set near the beginning of production. More often than not the publisher of a game dictates the target platforms themselves, rather than shopping their product to various platforms to pick up like in film.
